documents.abstract: Generative AI integration places teacher education at a critical crossroads for support teachers, whose identity is grounded in an ethics of care (Booth & Ainscow, 2008; d'Alonzo, 2017). The AIL framework requires holding the tension between innovation and relational pedagogy (Adamoli et al., 2026), as opposed to uncritical adoption (Chan & Lee, 2023; Williamson, 2024) or the Frankenstein Complex: resistance rooted in fear that AI impoverishes teaching's relational core (Selwyn, 2019). No prior study has jointly examined inclusive attitudes and AI co-agency in TFA Sostegno trainees. The general objective was to examine whether inclusive orientation predicts professional AI coagency. (RO1) Profile both constructs through cluster analysis; (RO2) test their relationship controlling for demographics; (RO3) test Deprivation as mediator of Concerns–Affordance via bootstrap (Preacher & Hayes, 2008). H1: Attitudes + Capability/Affordance (Ertmer, 2005). The essay is part of the growing body of research on artificial intelligence in educational setting, focusing on the transformation of the emotional and relational aspect of generative and conversational system. Starting from the research question regarding how the recent educational literature conceptualizes, discusses and problematizes the emotional support mediated by artificial intelligence and its relationship between embodied care and human educational relationships, the study adopts a comparative review approach to analyse the different ways in which these dimensions are defined, articulated, and problematized. The analysis examines scientific publications released between 2022 and 2026, a timeframe that corresponds to the most intense period of dissemination and accessibility of artificial intelligence systems, capable of simulating dialogical interaction, emotional support, affective personalization in the educational context. Through a strict and transparent selection process conducted on major international databases, in particular Scopus, Web of Science and PsycINFO, the study constructs a heterogeneous corpus of empirical studies, theoretical contributions and reviews that share a focus on the socio-emotional dimension of education mediated by artificial intelligence. documents.abstract: The evolution of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reconfiguring educational systems, reshaping the tenets of knowledge and the relational dynamics of instructional practice. Within this transition, computational AI's evolution reconfigures educational systems, altering classroom ecology, dismantling vertical knowledge transmission, and shifting assessment toward higher-order skills (Luckin, 2018; Selwyn, 2019). Adopting a Critical AI Literacy framework (Veldhuis et al., 2025), this study emphasizes understanding algorithmic agency, ethical impacts, and algorithmic justice. Critical oversight operations rest on the Human-in-Command principle (Floridi, 2022), asserting assessment as a human prerogative rooted in a student's biography. This fosters an "augmented intelligence" where routine-free time enhances educational relationships, mitigating cognitive passivity from chatbots (Andler, 2024). Ultimately, Digital Affective Literacy empowers teachers as pedagogical directors of care (Pellerey, 2024). The study adopted a convergent parallel mixed methods design to analyse teachers' perceptions and self-efficacy levels regarding AI. The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence in educational contexts has transformed how students encounter academic content, yet a fundamental question remains underexamined: Do English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners possess the critical literacy competencies needed to evaluate AI-generated texts? This study investigated whether students in Morocco’s Classes Préparatoires aux Grandes Écoles (CPGE)—one of the nation’s most academically selective post-secondary programs—demonstrate readiness for AI-era literacy demands. We developed a diagnostic assessment instrument, the Critical Reading Diagnostic Assessment (CRDA), designed to mirror common characteristics of AI-generated academic content: a confident, authoritative tone, a logical structure with subtle gaps, claims requiring verification, and culturally embedded assumptions. Thirty first-year CPGE students (M age = 18.6 years) evaluated argumentative passages across five critical dimensions: argument identification, evidence evaluation, assumption recognition, multi-source synthesis, and source criticism. Metacognitive self-assessment data were also collected. Results revealed systematic evaluation failures across all dimensions, with mean accuracy rates of only 18–39% and large effect sizes confirming substantial deficits (d = 1.11–2.25). Metacognitive analysis showed that students overestimated their abilities by 11–38 percentage points across all dimensions, indicating profound self-assessment inaccuracies.

Generative AI tools have moved rapidly into professional and organizational practice, outpacing individuals' capacity to use them well. Fluent, superficially convincing outputs foster automation bias, the tendency to over-rely on automated systems and miss the errors they introduce (Goddard et al., 2012); field-experimental evidence shows AI assistance boosts performance within its current capability while just as reliably degrading it outside that boundary, a limit users cannot detect from fluency alone (Dell'Acqua et al., 2023; Fernandes et al., 2026). This motivates closer scrutiny of how AI literacy is measured. Most existing instruments rely entirely on self-report, including for the cognitive dimension (Ng et al., 2024), and show weak correlations with independently developed objective performance tests (Koch et al., 2024), with self-assessment errors that are not uniformly directional (Zhang et al., 2026). documents.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence into educational ecosystems does not merely constitute an instrumental addition; rather, it portends an ontological transformation that reconfigures contemporary regimes of truth, epistemic validation criteria, and processes of subjectification (Paparella, Mancarella, 2025). The core issue extends beyond evaluating whether algorithmic tools are beneficial or detrimental; instead, it demands an understanding of the structural conditions under which education can still authentically occur when the production of knowledge is structurally outsourced to predictive and automated systems. Within this conceptual landscape, the paradigm of the algorithmic self comes to the fore: an inflection of personal identity that is continuously co-constituted and reconfigured within a perpetual relational dialogue with digital technologies. Governed by the underlying logics of recommendation, profiling, and automated personalization, the algorithmic self is exposed to a progressive semantic impoverishment. The rapid adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) decision systems has increased organizational dependence on large-scale data, making big data governance a critical requirement for ensuring reliable and responsible decision-making. Although AI systems are often evaluated based on predictive accuracy and computational performance, their trustworthiness is strongly influenced by the quality, security, privacy, traceability, and fairness of the data used throughout the AI lifecycle. This study aims to develop a Big Data Governance Framework for Trustworthy AI Decision Systems by integrating key governance dimensions with trustworthy AI requirements. A qualitative conceptual framework development approach was employed, supported by structured literature review, thematic synthesis, and design science research principles. Relevant literature on big data governance, trustworthy AI, data quality, privacy, security, explainability, accountability, fairness, and AI decision systems was reviewed to identify recurring concepts and research gaps. The results show that trustworthy AI decision systems require seven core governance dimensions: data quality governance, security and privacy governance, metadata and data lineage, bias and fairness control, explainability support, accountability mechanisms, and continuous monitoring. These dimensions strengthen trustworthy AI capabilities, including reliability, transparency, explainability, fairness, privacy preservation, security, robustness, and auditability. The proposed framework demonstrates that trustworthy AI is not only determined by algorithmic performance but also by strong data governance across the AI lifecycle. This study concludes that effective big data governance can improve decision accuracy, traceability, accountability, risk reduction, and stakeholder trust in AI-based decision systems.

Safety in trauma and surgical critical care is inseparable from the reliability of communication at transitions of care. Handoffs are recurrent, high-risk moments in which teams transfer not only information but responsibility, prioritization, uncertainty, and contingency planning; failures at these points propagate into omissions, delayed escalation, and preventable harm to patients and strain on the workforce. Structured handoff tools improve completeness and clarity but inconsistently change hard clinical endpoints, and tools alone do not create the culture of safety on which high-reliability organizations (HROs) depend. This narrative review synthesizes civilian handoff research, human-factors and HRO theory, situation-awareness, psychological safety, trauma video review, and military medical lessons-learned into a single implementable framework for safer trauma and surgical intensive care unit (SICU) transitions. We propose a 5-stage communication cycle: (1) teams Brief before transfer to establish roles, a shared mental model, and anticipate threats; (2) Handoff using a structured tool matched to the transition; (3) Backbrief so the receiver synthesizes high-risk items and ownership; (4) Threat Forecast to state explicitly what may deteriorate and what triggers escalation; and (5) Post-hoc Review to convert selected transitions into learning. The stages map onto HRO hallmarks and depend on psychological safety, deference to expertise, and the inclusion of nurses and other frontline staff whose voices and well-being are integral to safe transitions. Because rare clinical endpoints are difficult to attribute, we offer a layered measurement framework spanning process, team-behavior, documentation, clinical, and workforce-culture measures. Reframing the handoff from a single script into a repeatable, high-reliability communication cycle offers trauma and SICU teams a scalable, adaptable strategy for enhancing safer health care systems.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is profoundly transforming how individuals communicate, learn, and build relationships. In education, its impact extends beyond technology, reshaping the construction of meaning and the experience of encounters with others. The pedagogical question, therefore, concerns not only what artificial intelligence is capable of doing but also what risks being redefined when relationships are interpreted according to the criteria of efficiency, immediacy, and functionality (Panciroli & Rivoltella, 2023). Accordingly, although generative systems are now capable of simulating forms of dialogue, listening, and apparently empathic support, it becomes essential to distinguish the simulation of relationships from genuine relational experience. The production of coherent and personalized responses does not, in fact, entail responsibility, reciprocity, vulnerability, or participation in a shared history. It is precisely this distinction that makes care an indispensable interpretative category for understanding the meaning of contemporary education. Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly entering educational practice as a tool for producing texts, designing materials and supporting instructional decisions. Its presence, though, does not concern only technical efficiency. It also affects the way educational language is perceived, especially when a message appears empathic, reassuring and pedagogically appropriate. The question addressed in this study is not whether AI can write correct educational responses, but whether such responses are recognized as expressions of care when their authorship is uncertain or attributed to either a teacher or an artificial system. Care is understood here not as emotional tone alone, but as a pedagogical relation grounded in attention, responsibility and situated judgment (Noddings, 2005). The study adopts an exploratory mixed-methods design with a quantitatively driven structure and an integrated qualitative component. An anonymous online questionnaire was administered to 807 participants enrolled in teacher qualification pathways at Link Campus University. Background: The integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into creative practice raises new questions for craft-based disciplines such as ceramic design, where digital ideation must ultimately be translated into physical, material form. Objectives: This study explores (RQ1) where and why the alignment of AI-generated concept imagery with hand-built ceramic outcomes fails; (RQ2) how prompt-based iteration with a general-purpose text-to-image model supports or hinders the progressive refinement of a single design; and (RQ3) what forms of human knowledge and intervention are necessary to translate AI-generated concepts into producible ceramic objects. Methods: Using a qualitative, practice-based methodology, the researcher employed a text-to-image generative AI tool (ChatGPT 4 Plus + DALL·E 3) to generate design concepts for three ceramic objects—a children’s plate, a house number plaque, and a wall panel—which were subsequently produced by hand in collaboration with a professional ceramic instructor. Results: In the hands of a designer with limited ceramic experience, production difficulties clustered where the AI image encoded constraints that were invisible to the prompt—contour line weight, color separation in small recesses, lettering, scale and modular tolerance. AI-generated alternatives were frequently visually compelling yet materially infeasible, and the tool could not support incremental refinement of a single design across prompts. Whether these failures reflect properties of the AI output or the maker’s skill ceiling cannot be fully separated in a single-operator study; what follows is therefore a provisional, criteria-stated attribution, in which each breakdown is assigned to its most plausible source and the residual uncertainty is flagged. Conclusion: Generative AI functioned as a co-creative ideation partner rather than an autonomous designer; the negotiation between AI-proposed imagery and material reality was carried out by the human maker, drawing on codified technical knowledge (firing, shrinkage, dimensions) as well as tacit, embodied skill (brushwork, contouring, judging what will “work in clay”).

ChatGPT has become a part of the second language (L2) writing process as learners brainstorm ideas, seek feedback, and revise their texts. However, its pedagogical value depends on whether these interactions sustain behavioural, cognitive, and affective student engagement or contribute to disengagement. This systematic review synthesises research on ChatGPT-assisted L2 writing in the context of higher education concerning student engagement, examining patterns in research methods, theoretical perspectives, thematic findings, and future directions. The findings indicate that ChatGPT may both support and constrain student engagement, depending on learner characteristics, task design, feedback quality, and teacher guidance. The included studies highlighted that behaviourally, learners participated in planning and revision, but some relied heavily on artificial intelligence (AI) generated suggestions. Cognitively, ChatGPT prompted feedback evaluation and reflection, while inaccurate responses and cognitive offloading could limit deeper engagement. Affectively, learners reported motivation and reduced writing anxiety alongside frustration and a lack of interpersonal support. To organise the factors associated with both engagement and disengagement, the review proposes the preliminary ChatGPT-Enabled Smart Learning Environment (CESLE) framework which integrates engagement and disengagement factors and advances the concept of Ethical Human–AI Synergy through algorithmic stewardship, ethical collaborative intelligence, and an AI + teacher approach. The framework offers a context-sensitive foundation for supporting learner agency, responsible AI use, and sustained engagement in ChatGPT-assisted L2 writing. Thus, the review underscores the need for teacher-guided integration of AI that supports learners’ critical judgement and authorial voice.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming teaching and learning in Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) by providing personalized instructional support and improving access to learning resources. However, growing reliance on AI tools may reduce learners’ cognitive effort, leading to cognitive displacement with potential implication for student engagement and knowledge retention. This study investigated the extent of AI tool usage, the level of cognitive effort displacement, and the relationships among AI tool usage, cognitive effort displacement, student engagement, and knowledge retention among TVET students in Abia State, Nigeria. A descriptive correlational survey design was adopted. The study population comprised 2,400 TVET students, from which a sample of 343 respondents was selected using multistage sampling techniques. Data were collected using the Cognitive Effort Displacement, Engagement, and Retention Questionnaire (CEDERQ) (α = 0.85). Mean and standard deviation were used to answer the research questions, while Pearson product-moment correlation was employed to test the hypotheses at the 0.05 level of significance. The findings revealed a high level of AI tool usage (x̄ = 3.47), a moderate to high level of cognitive effort displacement (x̄ = 3.26), and a high level of student engagement and knowledge retention (x̄ = 3.32). AI tool usage showed a significant positive relationship with cognitive effort displacement (r = 0.612, p < 0.05), whereas cognitive effort displacement had significant negative relationships with student engagement (r = –0.478, p < 0.05) and knowledge retention (r = –0.563, p < 0.05). The study concludes that while AI-assisted learning enhances instructional support in TVET, excessive dependence on AI may undermine active cognitive engagement and long-term knowledge retention. The study recommends pedagogical approaches that balance AI support with independent problem-solving and reflective learning.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) offers opportunities to transform organizational learning and strengthen sustainable development. However, existing research often examines AI capability, organizational learning, digital innovation strategy, and sustainability separately. This study aims to develop an integrated conceptual framework explaining how AI-enabled organizational learning may contribute to sustainable organizational development. An integrative literature review was conducted using structured searches of Scopus, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect, supplemented by citation tracking through Google Scholar. Thirty-one scholarly sources were synthesized according to their theoretical constructs, explanatory mechanisms, and levels of analysis. The framework integrates the Resource-Based View, Dynamic Capability Theory, Technology-Organization-Environment framework, and technology acceptance theories. The study proposes an Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Learning Ecosystem (AILE) framework comprising four direct propositions linking AI Capability, AI-Enabled Learning Ecosystem, Digital Innovation Strategy, and Sustainable Organizational Development. Two additional propositions identify employee engagement and technology acceptance, alongside resource efficiency and AI governance, as moderating conditions. The framework also introduces organizational sustainability indicators, a resource cost-benefit assessment, and a four-stage implementation roadmap. The proposed framework offers a theoretical foundation for examining how AI-supported learning can contribute to organizational resilience, workforce development, and responsible digital innovation. Its potential relevance extends to SDGs 4, 8, and 9. As the framework remains conceptual, longitudinal and multilevel empirical studies are required to validate the proposed relationships and assess their practical effectiveness.

Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) may support early detection and clinical decision-making of oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs), but clinical implementation depends on dentists’ acceptance of AI-assisted clinical decision support. This study aimed to identify structural associations of AI acceptance among dentists using an extended Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 500 dentists. Construct validity and reliability were assessed using confirmatory factor analysis. Hypothesized associations were evaluated using structural equation modeling with bootstrap mediation analysis. The extended TAM showed generally satisfactory measurement properties and good overall model fit. Attitude toward AI showed the strongest association with behavioral intention (β = 0.550), followed by AI-assisted clinical decision reliance (β = 0.220), perceived usefulness (β = 0.180), trust (β = 0.140), and perceived ease of use (β = 0.120). Significant indirect effects operated through attitude toward AI. The model explained 67.5% of the variance in behavioral intention. Dentists reported favorable behavioral intention toward AI-assisted decision support for OPMD detection. Attitude toward AI showed the strongest association with behavioral intention. The findings are consistent with the extended TAM. Successful implementation will require explainable systems, clinician education, trust-building, and effective workflow integration. Longitudinal studies are needed to determine whether these associations translate into actual clinical adoption. Understanding factors associated with dentists’ acceptance of AI may support the responsible integration of AI-assisted decision support into oral cancer screening pathways.

documents.abstract: Abstract Integrating generative artificial intelligence within game-based learning offers promising but still-maturing possibilities for computational thinking (CT) education. This developmental research study (Type I) reports the design and preliminary validation of an AI-enhanced game-based learning environment (AI-GBLE) for upper-secondary students. Grounded in constructivism, cognitive load theory, information processing theory, mental models theory, and game-based learning principles, the environment integrates six components on the Roblox platform—problem-based scenarios, learning resources, collaborative learning, a CT enhancement centre, scaffolding, and an AI coaching system combining a GPT-4-powered conversational non-player character with a rule-based adaptive difficulty engine—within an authentic Smart Greenhouse (Internet of Things) context. Following expert appraisal of content, instructional design, and media-technology quality by nine specialists, three per domain, 30 Grade 11 students in Thailand used the environment across eight 60-minute sessions over six weeks in a one-group pretest–posttest validation. Students showed pre–post gains of 3.07 points on the 20-point computational thinking test (Wilcoxon r = .86; Cohen’s d_av = 2.79) and 5.90 points on the 15-point achievement test (d_av = 3.23)—standardised effects inflated by ceiling compression—and reported strong immediate satisfaction across six acceptance dimensions (overall M = 4.64). Because the single-group design precludes causal attribution, these findings are interpreted as preliminary evidence—of feasibility, acceptability, and learning-related signals from a developed prototype—rather than as intervention effectiveness. The individual contributions of the AI coach, adaptive engine, and other components were not empirically established. The study contributes a theory-mapped design heuristic for AI-augmented game-based learning and identifies controlled comparisons, improved measurement, and mechanism-focused analyses as priorities for subsequent research.

The pedagogical question concerns the quality of the training experience when artificial responses become ordinary learning practices. The article presents digital affective literacy as a necessary skill for engaging with AI ethically, through critical judgment and responsibility, in continuity with developments in AI literacy and its affective domain (Cuomo, Biagini, & Ranieri, 2022; Pretorius & Cahusac de Caux, 2024). The theoretical framework integrates AI in education, AI literacy, ethics of educational technologies, pedagogical care, teacher reflexivity, flipped learning, and Universal Design for Learning (UDL). The literature recognises the potential of AI for personalisation, accessibility, and study support, while recalling the role of educational mediation in preserving students' judgment (UNESCO, 2023). documents.abstract: Physical Education (PE) represents an emotionally rich learning environment where students experience continuous interactions, feedback loops, and embodied activities that strongly shape motivation, self-efficacy, and social participation. In recent years, this context has been increasingly influenced by digital technologies and emerging artificial intelligence (AI) systems. International evidence indicates that the combination of digital tools and social-emotional learning (SEL) pathways can significantly enhance students' outcomes in PE, supporting motivation, engagement, and inclusive participation (Saqinah et al., 2025). At the same time, a recent scoping review of 63 studies highlights that SEL development in PE remains theoretically fragmented and only partially aligned with the main pedagogical models adopted in the field (Dyson et al., 2021). This gap suggests the need for frameworks capable of integrating emotional, relational, and technological dimensions in a coherent and ethically grounded manner. documents.abstract: This study investigates how digital financial literacy, perceived transparency of artificial intelligence advisory services, investment and wealth knowledge, and cyber-risk self-protection shape Perceived Private Wealth Management Capability (PWMC) among digitally engaged retail investors in an emerging-market context. PWMC is conceptualized as a self-assessed capability outcome rather than an objective indicator of wealth-management performance, portfolio returns, or private-banking status. Drawing on the financial capability framework, trust in automation theory, and protection motivation theory, the study develops a trust-to-capability model in which trust in hybrid artificial intelligence advisory and digital wealth management behavior serves as a key explanatory mechanism. A non-probability sample of 249 digitally engaged retail investors in Vietnam was analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling in SmartPLS 4.1, with 5,000 bootstrap subsamples. The results show that digital financial literacy is the strongest antecedent of trust in hybrid artificial intelligence advisory (β = 0.517, p < 0.001). At the same time, perceived advisory transparency also exerts a significant positive effect (β = 0.261, p < 0.001). Investment and wealth knowledge emerged as the strongest predictor of digital wealth management behavior (β = 0.348, p < 0.001). Trust, digital wealth management behavior, and investment and wealth knowledge each positively influence perceived private wealth management capability. Digital wealth management behavior partially mediates the effects of trust, investment, and wealth knowledge on perceived capability. Cyber-risk self-protection limited evidence of a boundary condition by strengthening the relationship between trust and digital wealth management behavior. However, the effect size is small and should be interpreted cautiously (β = 0.098, p = 0.038). The model explains 60.2% of the variance in digital wealth management behavior and 44.3% of the variance in perceived private wealth management capability. By moving beyond conventional explanations of robo-advisory adoption and technology acceptance, this study theorizes hybrid AI advisory as a calibrated trust environment in which retail investors’ perceived capability depends not only on whether they trust AI-supported advice but also on whether that trust translates into protective, enacted digital wealth management behavior. The findings should be interpreted in the context of digitally engaged retail investors. They should not be generalized to private banking clients, high-net-worth investors, objective portfolio performance, or verified wealth outcomes.

Purpose: This paper analyses how digital tools such as artificial intelligence, predictive analytics, and digital twin technologies can enhance risk assessment and decision-making in business operations. Design/Methodology/Approach: The research studies the existing literature on digital transformation and risk management, drawing on 29 publications from 2020 to 2026 (27 journal articles published in the Scopus database and two book chapters). The publications are analysed using thematic synthesis based on three constructs: digital tools, risk assessment capability, and decision-making performance. Research Limitation: The study is based on existing literature, indicating the need for further research on the practical implementation of digital technologies in different business environments. Findings: The results suggest that introducing digital technologies into management systems speeds decision-making, improves risk management, and makes organisations more competitive. Digital technologies enable organisations to process large amounts of real-time data, detect potential risks, and support more informed, timely managerial decisions. Practical Implication: The findings show that digital tools can improve risk assessment procedures and support more effective managerial decision-making. Social Implication: More efficient decision-making and risk management contribute to greater organisational resilience in dynamic business environments. Originality/Value: The study addresses two gaps in the literature: insufficient analysis of technology combinations and the human factor. In its tool-to-capability framework, digital tools contribute to operational performance indirectly by affecting risk assessment and decision-making, an effect the synthesis links to governance and managerial competencies.

In the ongoing AI boom—now supercharged by large language models and generative AI tools—the rapid integration of AI into health care and public health has created an urgent need for professionals who combine deep domain expertise (clinical, epidemiological, ethical, and contextual expertise in health and public health) with AI fluency (the ability to understand, critically evaluate, use, and oversee AI systems effectively). Without domain guidance, AI risks producing biased, unsafe, or contextually irrelevant outputs that compromise patient safety and exacerbate disparities. Conversely, domain experts lacking AI fluency may underuse or misuse these technologies, missing opportunities to improve care quality, operational efficiency, and population health. A foundational understanding of the modern AI system stack—comprising energy, accelerators, infrastructure, models, and applications—empowers health professionals to make informed decisions on adoption, evaluation, governance, and ethical use without needing to code or build models themselves. This stack framework highlights critical interdependencies and health care–specific challenges, including regulatory compliance, data privacy, sustainability, and resource constraints, particularly in low- and middle-income settings. This paper argues that cultivating domain-AI bilingualism is essential for safe, effective, and equitable AI integration worldwide. It outlines the 5-layer AI system stack applied to health care, key reasons for hybrid expertise, and a practical 4-step pathway: awakening (recognizing AI’s transformative role), intrepidity (courageously engaging foundational AI concepts), bilingualism (translating between clinical needs and AI capabilities), and visionary leadership (driving organizational and policy readiness). It outlines major barriers, targeted strategies, and recommendations for educators, institutions, and policymakers. By bridging domain knowledge with AI fluency, health professionals can direct—rather than be directed by—AI technologies, including emerging agentic systems, toward more precise, sustainable, and human-centered outcomes while mitigating risks. This hybrid capability represents a nonnegotiable competency for the health workforce for thriving in the post-2026 AI era.

documents.abstract: Dynamic Personalized Guidance Architecture (Dynamic PGA) is a human-centered conceptual framework for continuously adaptive AI experiences. The framework explores how artificial intelligence might adapt not only to an individual's longer-range goals, interests, knowledge, and preferences, but also to meaningful changes that occur as an experience unfolds. The paper introduces a developing Dynamic A/B model: Dynamic A provides adaptive direction around the individual's goals and intended destination, while Dynamic B introduces state-aware responsiveness to the individual's immediate circumstances. Together, they express a central principle of the framework: A remembers the destination. B respects the human being who has to get there. Version 1.0 explores potential applications in education, experiential travel, professional environments, healthcare communication, and creative work, while emphasizing human agency, privacy, appropriate boundaries, and future research and validation.

documents.abstract: Purpose: To examine the relationship between economic sustainability, innovation, and sustainable development as key determinants of the resilience of modern economic systems and identify strategic approaches for strengthening resilience through digital transformation. Design/Methodology/Approach: The study employed a qualitative research design based on a systematic review of scientific literature, comparative analysis, and conceptual synthesis. The review covered 31 studies (2020–2026) retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus, supplemented by Google Scholar, and identified the principal mechanisms that enhance the adaptability and long-term stability of economic systems. Research Limitation: The study is conceptual and based on secondary sources. Future research should validate the proposed framework using empirical evidence from different sectors. Findings: The results show that economic sustainability is closely linked to integrating technological and digital innovations into production and management processes. Structural adaptability, system integration, stakeholder participation, human capital development, and effective resource management were identified as key prerequisites for sustainable growth and resilience. Automation, digitalisation, and artificial intelligence improve business processes, increase operational efficiency, and support sustainable development by integrating economic, environmental, and social objectives. Practical Implication: The findings guide policymakers and business leaders in designing innovation-driven strategies that enhance economic resilience. Social Implication: Strengthening economic sustainability promotes long-term stability, social well-being, environmental responsibility, and resilience. Originality/Value: The study integrates the established constructs of economic sustainability, innovation, digital transformation, and resilience into one framework; what is new is the crisis-digital paradigm, which treats digital tools as a system-forming element of resilience management.

The rapid development of digital technology makes it important for young learners to become familiar with the basic concepts of artificial intelligence (AI). This community service activity introduced basic AI concepts to 28 Grade VI students at State Elementary School 26, Bengkulu City, on 27 August 2026, through interactive lectures, educational games, question-and-answer sessions, and simple demonstrations. Descriptive observations of student participation during the activities indicated enthusiasm and engagement with examples of AI, its benefits, and its risks. No formal evaluation instrument, pre-test/post-test scores, or numerical outcome measurements were available; therefore, the extent of learning improvement cannot be quantified. The activity provides an initial model for introducing age-appropriate AI literacy in elementary schools.

Digital assessment has become a strategic component of online higher education, supporting not only the certification of learning outcomes but also feedback processes, student monitoring and quality assurance (JISC, 2020). Recent technological developments have expanded the possibilities of assessment through Artificial Intelligence (AI), learning analytics and immersive technologies, which are increasingly associated with personalised feedback, adaptive assessment, data-informed decision making and authentic learning experiences (Holmes et al., 2023; Kamalov et al., 2023). While the educational potential of these technologies has been widely discussed, less attention has been devoted to their institutional formalisation. Technological innovation does not automatically translate into institutional adoption. Universities may experiment with innovative tools without integrating them into policies, governance structures, assessment strategies or quality assurance systems. For this reason, understanding how emerging technologies are represented within institutional documentation can provide valuable insights into the maturity of digital assessment ecosystems. This article argues that older adults’ engagement with healthcare systems supported by artificial intelligence (AI) cannot be explained solely by access to technology or individual levels of digital literacy. The central claim is that when older adults are unable to benefit fully from these systems, the problem is often framed as a personal failure to adapt, whereas the deeper issue is a form of sociotechnical exclusion produced at the intersection of data representation, design norms, limited explainability, inadequate institutional support, and age-based bias. To explore this issue, the article draws on a composite case involving an older woman who struggles to use an AI-supported chronic disease monitoring application. It first examines the opportunities associated with artificial intelligence in the care of older adults and the conceptual tensions surrounding these technologies. It then presents the composite case and analyses it through the lenses of digital exclusion, digital ageism, participatory design, care ethics, and nursing practice. The article concludes that the success of artificial intelligence in healthcare should be assessed not only in terms of accuracy, speed, and efficiency, but also in terms of its capacity to involve older adults in care processes in ways that are understandable, safe, fair, and dignified.

Generative artificial intelligence offers new opportunities to strengthen self-directed learning in nursing education when its integration is supported by a structured pedagogical design. This study aimed to evaluate the effect of the E-PAGIA strategy, organized into planning, construction, self-monitoring, and interaction/transfer stages, on self-directed learning among nursing students. A quantitative, quasi-experimental, longitudinal study was conducted with 128 students, distributed between an experimental group and a control group, with 64 participants in each. The intervention lasted eight weeks. Self-directed learning was assessed using the Self-Directed Learning Instrument, considering both the overall score and its dimensions. The groups showed comparable baseline scores. Following the intervention, the experimental group increased its mean overall score from 65.00 to 82.35 points, whereas the control group increased from 65.75 to 69.46. Improvements in the experimental group were observed across all four dimensions and were particularly pronounced in learning motivation and planning and implementation. Analysis adjusted for baseline scores confirmed significant differences between groups and showed a large effect associated with the strategy. The findings indicate that E-PAGIA can foster self-directed learning when generative artificial intelligence is integrated as cognitive support within a pedagogical sequence that preserves students' intellectual responsibility, teacher mediation, and critical verification of information. The study concludes that E-PAGIA represents a relevant pedagogical innovation for nursing education.

documents.abstract: This review covers human–artificial intelligence collaboration in making decisions, observing how scholarship has moved from thinking of AI as a passive tool to considering it as an active actor in healthcare, management, and ethics. While AI systems provide for efficient data processing and pattern recognition, humans provide contextual understanding, ethical judgment, creativity, and accountability. Previous literature suggests that well-designed collaboration between humans and AI may outperform completely automated decision-making. However, several key challenges persist, like bias, lack of transparency, miscalibrated trust, poorly defined distribution of roles, and accountability gaps. To handle these concerns, human-centered design, explainability in AI, well-articulated guidelines on ethical consideration, and mechanisms that effectively introduce oversight remain at the core of literature. These approaches jointly try to ensure that human–AI decision-making systems are fair, accountable, and trustworthy in high-stakes and critical settings

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) in finance has evolved from statistical learning and machine learning for structured prediction, through deep learning and foundation models for representation learning, language understanding, and reasoning, to retrieval-augmented generation for knowledge-grounded reasoning and agentic AI for autonomous planning and execution. In this paper, we examine how researchers and practitioners can select and apply AI methods in finance. We first show that the major paradigms of financial AI address fundamentally different classes of problems, rather than forming a strict hierarchy of capability. We then review the current state of research on AI in finance and trace how these paradigms have reshaped financial data, financial tasks, decision support, and human-AI collaboration. Building on this, we propose practical guidelines for matching AI paradigms to task characteristics, and show that more advanced models, such as foundation models or autonomous agents, are not universally superior. We conclude by outlining open challenges for researchers and practitioners working toward reliable financial AI.

Mental-health strain has become a routine feature of organizational life, yet managers and organizations continue to struggle to explain why capable employees make avoidable errors, why teams lose coordination under pressure, and why judgment quality deteriorates during periods of sustained stress. This article argues that executive function decay—the temporary or chronic degradation of working memory, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility—is a central but underrecognized mechanism linking mental strain to workplace performance failures.Drawing on research from cognitive neuroscience, clinical psychology, and organizational behavior, I explain how common forms of mental-health morbidity and burnout impair the cognitive capacities that support judgment, emotional regulation, and adaptive decision-making. I show how executive function decay produces predictable patterns of managerial behavior, team dysfunction, and organizational drift that are misattributed to motivation, attitude, or character.The article introduces a multilevel framework connecting executive function impairment to outcomes at the individual, team, and organizational levels. I then translate this framework into practical implications for leaders and HR systems, highlighting how job design, leadership behavior, workload architecture, and organizational norms can either stabilize or erode cognitive capacity. By reframing mental health as a decision-quality and organizational design issue, this article offers managers and scholars a practical lens for improving judgment, coordination, and resilience under pressure.

This paper explores the integration of artificial intelligence (AI), automation, and advanced digital tools within modern policing frameworks. By analyzing current implementations—including predictive policing algorithms, automated facial recognition, automated license plate readers (ALPRs), and AI-driven evidence management systems—this study assesses how these technologies enhance operational efficiency, accelerate response times, and optimize resource allocation. Furthermore, the paper addresses critical systemic challenges, specifically targeting algorithmic bias, citizen privacy concerns, data security vulnerabilities, and the regulatory frameworks required to govern automated decision-making. Ultimately, this research provides a balanced framework for law enforcement executives and policymakers, demonstrating how agencies can leverage cutting-edge technical innovation while upholding the core principles of ethical, transparent, and community-oriented justice

Abstract Judicial artificial intelligence requires grounds for warranted reliance rather than confidence alone. This study examines how respondents in Bangladesh distinguish understandable reasons, independent validation and opportunities to challenge AI-supported recommendations. A cross-sectional analysis of 385 adult, AI-aware respondents uses seven questionnaire items without treating their mixed normative and conditional wording as a validated explainability-trust scale. The analysis combines paired endorsement comparisons, proportional-odds models with robust covariance, multiplicity adjustment and paired-outcome coefficient comparisons. Independent-validation-contingent trust was endorsed by 247 respondents (64.2%), compared with 215 (55.8%) for explanation-contingent trust: a paired difference of 8.3 percentage points (95% bootstrap interval 1.6–15.1; Holm-adjusted p = .021). Access to review or appeal received greater endorsement than the ability to question recommendations (85.2% versus 65.2%; difference 20.0 points, 95% interval 14.3–25.7). None of the eight focal associations between four governance expectations and the two trust propositions remained distinguishable from zero after Holm adjustment. The joint test of differences between the four outcome-specific coefficients was also inconclusive (p = .236). These findings identify a descriptive separation between explanations, validation and remedies while providing limited adjusted evidence about how those expectations align within respondents. The predominantly student sample does not establish judicial practice, actual reliance or causal effects of explanations. The article develops a layered account of judicial AI governance that connects understandable reasons with independent evaluation and effective review, and specifies a measurement and experimental agenda for testing calibrated reliance.

documents.abstract: This study examined the feasibility of an artificial intelligence system using webcam eye tracking to estimate sustained attention performance. In a controlled laboratory study, 129 participants (mean age: 25.98 ± 2.07 years; 83.7% female) completed the AX Continuous Performance Task. Performance was operationalized as a reciprocal-log index of correct-response reaction time, with higher values indicating faster responses. Six visual scanning features were captured, and five composite models were compared: one literature-based and four derived from experimental data. All showed significant in-sample associations with performance. The weighted composite incorporating all six features provided the best in-sample fit, but participant-level split-half cross-validation yielded a modest out-of-sample association (r = 0.19). Univariate analyses linked better performance to faster jumps and lower length and speed irregularity. These findings provide preliminary evidence for webcam-derived gaze features in cognitive assessment under laboratory conditions, with further validation needed before integration into human–computer interaction applications.

documents.abstract: With the pervasive integration of generative artificial intelligence across diverse social domains, user acceptance intention manifests a distinctive coexistence of "fun and fear." Grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model, this investigation develops an expanded model by integrating perceived enjoyment, AI anxiety, and privacy concerns, whilst assessing the moderating influence of professional background. Based on 486 valid questionnaires and structural equation modeling, the model shows acceptable fit (/df = 1.88, RMSEA = 0.043, CFI/TLI > 0.90). Perceived enjoyment strengthens attitude (β = 0.324, p < 0.001) and perceived usefulness (β = 0.284, p < 0.001), while AI anxiety reduces perceived usefulness (β = -0.296, p < 0.001) and privacy concern weakens attitude (β = -0.148, p = 0.021); the core TAM path is supported (ATT BI: β = 0.643, p < 0.001; BI USE: β = 0.535, p < 0.001). By contrast, H7, H8, and H10 are not supported (p > 0.05), and professional background shows negligible moderation. These results suggest that promoting generative AI requires enhancing enjoyable interaction while reducing anxiety and privacy risks.

Abstract Background The rapid integration of generative AI (GenAI) into nursing education has prompted widespread concern about academic integrity and assessment validity. However, this dominant discourse may obscure a more fundamental challenge: preparing nursing students for clinical practice environments where AI already mediates triage, diagnostics, documentation, and clinical decision-making. Objective This integrative review examines how GenAI is conceptualized within the nursing education literature and investigates the extent to which current discourse addresses professional formation rather than academic compliance. Methods Following Whittemore and Knafl’s integrative review methodology, a systematic search of PubMed, Google Scholar, and SciSpace (Typeset) was conducted for literature published between January 2022 and February 2026. Two reviewers independently screened 456 records, with 119 papers meeting the inclusion criteria. The methodological quality of empirical studies was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). Corpus-level descriptive mapping quantified dominant themes and conceptual patterns, while an interpretive synthesis examined how GenAI was framed and the extent to which professional formation elements, including identity, moral agency, and clinical judgment, were addressed. Results Of the 119 unique studies analyzed, 84% (n=100) predominantly framed GenAI as a content-generation tool and academic integrity threat. Only 35.3% (n=42) conceptualized AI as a pedagogical tool, and a critical gap was identified in professional formation: identity formation was addressed in only 10% (n=12) of papers and moral agency in just 5% (n=6). Explicit acknowledgment that AI already routinely mediates frontline clinical decisions (eg, sepsis alerts and fall risk algorithms) in current practice settings was notably absent. The discourse emphasizes governance and faculty literacy, but sustained curricula addressing nurse identity in AI-mediated care remain underdeveloped. Conclusions Current nursing education discourse predominantly frames AI as a writing tool and an academic integrity concern, failing to prepare students for the algorithmic practice environments they will inhabit. Nursing education must reframe AI as a professional formation issue, explicitly addressing how algorithms reshape clinical judgment, moral agency, and professional identity.

documents.abstract: The rapid emergence of generative artificial intelligence (Gen AI) is reshaping human resource (HR) management, requiring HR managers to integrate traditional HR expertise with AI-specific competencies. Despite growing research on AI-enabled human resource management, few studies have identified the competencies required by hybrid HR–Gen AI managers, particularly in emerging-market contexts. This study aims to identify and analyze these competencies in the Tunisian context and to develop an empirically grounded competency framework for AI-enabled HR transformation. Under an interpretivist paradigm and an inductive, qualitative approach, 12 semistructured interviews were conducted with hybrid HR–Gen AI managers. Using the MAXQDA tool, thematic analysis identified 49 competency codes grouped into seven competency categories: strategic, change management, human and interpersonal, technological and technical, analytic, ethical, and basic competencies. Seven individual competencies were mentioned by more than 50% of respondents, while “Gen AI-driven HR task automation” and “data privacy and confidentiality management” were identified as the most frequently cited, with each identified by 10 of the 12 participants. The findings also point to the relevance of ethical awareness, critical thinking, and a human-centered mindset in managing Gen AI-enabled HR transformation. The proposed competency framework can inform HR workforce development and organizational strategies for the responsible and effective integration of Gen AI into HR practices.

Researchers commonly manipulate chatbot anthropomorphism through social cues, whose effects vary and may introduce unintended perceptual differences. Generative AI enables an alternative: manipulating perceived characteristics through natural-language prompting. Two online experiments (N = 84 each) evaluated behavior-prescriptive and perception-goal prompting for manipulating anthropomorphism. Study 1 found no significant differences in anthropomorphism. Study 2 found significant differences in general, mindful, and mindless anthropomorphism (ds = .86–.95), without significant differences in response coherence or perceived intelligence. These findings provide initial empirical support for perception-goal prompting and suggest broader methodological possibilities for manipulating perceived chatbot characteristics in human–AI communication research.

documents.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming the way individuals interact with digital technologies and Information Systems (IS), requiring a rethinking of some traditional assumptions underlying Human–Computer Interaction (HCI). In Management Information Systems (MIS), this transformation extends beyond the design of usable interfaces toward the development of intelligent systems that can actively support, augment, and collaborate with human users. This chapter examines the evolution from HCI to Human–AI Collaboration (HAC) and discusses its implications for the development of intelligent MIS. It first establishes the conceptual foundations of HCI, including human factors, user-centered design, usability, accessibility, and user experience (UX). It then examines the emergence of Human–AI Interaction (HAI) and the transition from computers as passive tools toward intelligent interaction partners. Building on this foundation, the chapter conceptualizes HAC through complementary human and AI capabilities, human oversight, AI-augmented decision-making, and increasingly autonomous AI systems. Particular attention is given to human-centered design, Generative AI, conversational and multimodal interfaces, intelligent UX, and the different roles humans may assume in AI-enabled environments, including interaction, evaluation, supervision, and, under appropriate conditions, collaboration with AI systems. The chapter further discusses ethical and organizational challenges, including algorithmic bias, privacy, transparency, accountability, automation bias, and human agency. It argues that the future of MIS will increasingly depend not only on technological intelligence but also on how effectively HAC is designed, governed, and integrated into organizational work.

Autonomous and AI-driven systems now issue operations whose consequences land far from where they were decided: in radio-access-network controllers, operator charging systems, device queues and DMA engines, robot actuators, emergency broadcast channels, payment rails, browsers, and long-running agent processes that migrate between hosts. Across all of these, a recurring failure appears. A system treats an acknowledgement, a status code, a callback, a log entry, or its own internal view as if it were proof that the intended effect occurred, on the intended target, under the conditions that were authorized. Observations are fused across mismatched clocks, identities, and configuration generations; agreements are treated as execution authority; partial effects are retried as if nothing happened; translated or transformed instructions are delivered as though they preserved their original meaning. This disclosure addresses that gap as a single architectural problem expressed across many domains. The disclosure presents a 280-page technical record comprising common-workflow flowcharts, phase-level engineering figures, implementation flowcharts, and 639 proposed patent claims. Its unifying principle is that the original authorized operation retains a stable identity from which every downstream representation, transformation, dispatch, acknowledgement, and observed effect must be separately reconstructed and qualified. Each workflow applies a conservative three-valued rule at every gate: all mandatory predicates supported advances; any predicate contradicted inhibits or raises an exception; any predicate unresolved holds. Final outcomes are expressed as scoped verdicts (CONSISTENT, INCONSISTENT, or UNRESOLVED) with the evidence, resource state, and gaps on which each verdict depends. Throughout, acknowledgement is distinguished from effect, observation from authority, eligibility from authorization, and historical records from current permission. The record is organized into technical groups, each with its own common workflow and claim set: Group A (claims 1–40) governs observation-to-control consistency in radio-access-network calculations: reconstructing resource identity and configuration generation, bounding temporal applicability under clock uncertainty, preserving measurement semantics across interfaces, selecting dependency-aware joint observations, maintaining consistency through controller migration and failover, and revalidating material dependencies before a control result is delivered. Group B (claims 41–80) addresses multi-agent network incident diagnosis and repair, covering source-qualified evidence provenance and independence, competing fault hypotheses resolved by discriminating evidence, repair-plan applicability under concurrent changes, asynchronous repair with partial-effect reconstruction, independent post-repair verification of recovery and adverse effects, and distributed incident history with recurrence analysis. Group C (claims 81–120) maintains telecommunications session lifecycle consistency across subscriber trust changes (SIM/eSIM), home and visited operator roaming and partial release, concurrent programmable quality-on-demand operations, user-plane usage, quota and charging lineage, purpose-scoped consent versus actual network effect, and partial operator outage with deferred settlement. Group D (claims 121–160) reconstructs hardware observation-to-effect consistency through independent hardware observers, CPU-to-device DMA memory continuity, device queue and descriptor occupancy, firmware and configuration invalidation, and cross-stage representation of external effects. Group E (claims 161–200) holds that negotiated agreement is not execution authority among multiple agents, covering versioned negotiation and partial acceptance, streaming artifacts and delegated sub-actions, amendment impact across versions, cancellation and late effects, partitioned participant views, and residual obligations at closure. Group F (claims 201–240) treats asynchronous tool and protocol operations, including durable task identity and callback origin, tool-schema generation and in-flight semantic change, acknowledged subscription and push-event coverage, resource alias and generation continuity, cancellation and retry with residual external effects, and concurrent usage-budget settlement. Group G (claims 241–280) translates machine-readable robot skills into calibration-qualified physical capability, evaluated by an independent safety controller, admitted under time-bounded command contracts, downgraded at runtime when capability degrades mid-actuation, transferred between robots without reusing unverified calibration, and closed by independent physical-effect observation. Group H (claims 281–320) carries emergency instructions from source to physical response: original instruction identity and provenance, extraction and preservation of safety-critical meaning, multilingual translation verification under uncertainty, recipient-specific exact-content dispatch, correction and supersession, and readback and response verification. Group M1 (claims 321–380) governs autonomous AI commerce from original purchase intent to actual commercial outcome, covering product, variant and seller continuity, complete monetary exposure at dynamic checkout, current purchasing authority, payment-mandate-to-financial-effect consistency, multi-agent shared budgets, and post-purchase fulfilment, refund, and correction. Group M2 (claims 381–440) operates at silicon level, binding an authorized operation to the hardware command a device actually consumes, through descriptor integrity, effective DMA translation and invalidation, reset and assignment incarnation, protected command admission with atomic use-state, shared quota admission, and cross-path effectuation coverage. Claims 441–509 extend the architecture to protected virtual-machine and sandbox runtimes with consequence-bound egress, dual-boundary digital-to-physical command enforcement, controller-local authority without transferable tokens, protected credential release, buffered physical-command invalidation, crash-resistant authority recovery, authority preservation across checkpoint, fork, migration and changing delegation, and separation of informative context from consequential execution. Group I (claims 510–539, with 600–639) secures browser and graphical-agent actions by binding an authorized task to the actual interface target, frame, origin, redirect, and background request it produces, and extends this to interface-independent control across graphical, voice, remote, native, and terminal interfaces. Group J (claims 540–599, with 600–639) preserves a persistent agent task’s logical identity, authority, outstanding external exposure, and callbacks across migration between execution instances, using generation fencing, representation-independent current authority, and callback-independent outcome verification, including treatment of partial and streaming effects without duplicate repetition. The material is offered as a public technical disclosure and reference architecture. The claims are proposed, not granted, and the figures describe implementation designs rather than guarantees of novelty, freedom to operate, or regulatory compliance. Safety-related content, including robotic and emergency-communication workflows, is non-certified and makes no SIL, PL, or standards-conformance claim. The record is intended for system architects, network and hardware engineers, AI-agent developers, standards contributors, and regulators concerned with accountable autonomy, where the question is not only whether an action was permitted, but whether what actually happened corresponds to what was authorized. documents.abstract: In increasingly complex and technology-rich educational environments, teachers are expected not only to master instructional strategies but also to critically interpret educational situations and make pedagogically informed decisions. Professional reflection has therefore become a fundamental component of teacher education, enabling educators to connect experience with pedagogical action (Dewey, 1933; Schön, 1983; Mortari, 2003). Within this perspective, the reflective journal functions as a self-narrative pedagogical device through which teachers reinterpret classroom situations, strengthening professional judgement and inclusive educational decision-making. From a narrative perspective, reflection transforms experience into meaning (Bruner, 1992). Digital storytelling has also been recognised as an effective strategy for fostering reflection and professional learning (Robin, 2008; Banzato, 2014; De Marco & Colazzo, 2021; Mazzini et al., 2025). At the same time, recent research has highlighted both the educational potential of generative AI and the need for its pedagogically grounded integration into teacher education (Holmes et al., 2019; Tan et al., 2025). The article addresses the topical issue of using generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in working with academic texts by combining practical work with GenAI, the analysis of dissertation abstracts, and the development of students’ critical attitudes toward AI-generated information. This study investigates the ability of generative artificial intelligence to reconstruct selected conceptual components of academic discourse without direct access to the corresponding dissertation abstract. The study analyzes contemporary scholarly approaches to the use of generative artificial intelligence in academic discourse. The aim of the study is to empirically determine the extent to which GenAI can reproduce the relevance, research aim, and research focus of an academic study based on a minimal set of input data. The methodology involved an experimental procedure with 25 undergraduate students enrolled in the program “Language and Literature (German). Translation” within the field of Germanic languages and literatures. The empirical material comprised 25 abstracts of successfully defended dissertations on Germanic linguistics. Two generative AI systems, ChatGPT and Gemini, were used in the experiment. Following a standardized prompting procedure, the systems were provided with the research topic, but the corresponding dissertation abstract was not made available to them. The AI-generated responses were compared with the corresponding conceptual components of the dissertation abstracts using comparative content analysis. The results indicate that GenAI can semantically reconstruct selected characteristics of an existing academic study, including its relevance, research aim, and focus. At the same time, the findings do not indicate textual copying of dissertation abstracts but rather suggest the possibility of reconstructing their content-related characteristics from limited input data. These results indicate the considerable potential of GenAI as a tool for supporting academic writing. Practical implications. The findings may be used to develop university curricula that establish a balanced approach to integrating generative artificial intelligence into the educational process while preserving fundamental principles of academic integrity and values.

Addressing how Generative AI (GenAI) reshapes the cognitive act of second language (L2) writing, this conceptual article draws on recent empirical literature (2023–2026). It grounds its analysis in the Cognitive Process Theory of Writing (CPTW), chosen because its decomposition of planning, translating, and reviewing under working-memory limits illuminates how cognitive labor is redistributed between learner and machine. Through CPTW, three key insights emerge. First, planning undergoes an externalization of productive struggle: offloading idea generation causes learners to bypass essential rhetorical problem framing. Second, translating experiences a voice constraint: model optimization toward conventionality flattens non-standard L2 syntax and homogenizes authorial voice. Third, reviewing suffers a reviewing bifurcation, splitting evaluation into goal-level appraisal and opaque decision-level monitoring. Theoretically, GenAI transforms writing into a co-generative sociotechnical practice requiring GenAI feedback literacy. Pedagogically, educators should adopt process-oriented assessments, using pre-prompting framing logs, annotated drafts, and prompt histories to evaluate cognitive engagement over polished final products.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping innovation management by moving beyond its conventional role as a technological tool toward becoming an active participant in creative and decision-making processes. This chapter examines how GenAI can function as a co-creator across the innovation process and explores the complementary roles of human and artificial intelligence in generating meaningful innovation outcomes. Adopting a structured integrative literature review approach, the study synthesizes recent research on GenAI-enabled innovation through thematic analysis and conceptual synthesis. The findings indicate that GenAI contributes across multiple stages of innovation, including opportunity recognition, idea generation and evaluation, product and service development, business model innovation, commercialization, and organizational innovation. Its primary strengths lie in rapid content generation, knowledge synthesis, recombination, scenario development, and iterative refinement, whereas human contributors remain central to problem framing, contextual interpretation, strategic and ethical judgment, validation, and accountability. Building on these complementary capabilities, the chapter proposes the Human–GenAI Innovation Co-Creation Framework, which conceptualizes innovation as an iterative cycle of framing, generating, evaluating, refining, validating, and experimenting. The analysis further identifies hallucination, bias and idea homogenization, intellectual property concerns, human over-reliance, AI literacy, and organizational governance as important boundary conditions shaping the effectiveness of co-creation. Overall, the chapter argues that the transformative potential of GenAI in innovation management lies not in replacing human innovators but in designing organizational processes that deliberately combine human judgment and creativity with GenAI’s generative and synthetic capabilities.

Abstract This study examines whether generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can improve university students’ mathematical problem-solving when it is designed not as an answer generator but as a metacognitive scaffold. Building on sociocultural scaffolding, self-regulated learning, and Pólya’s problem-solving model, the study tested a 15-week structured GenAI-supported intervention in Calculus I. A cluster-assigned quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test design was implemented with 128 undergraduates distributed across four tutorial sections: two sections used a Socratic GenAI protocol (n = 60), and two sections received traditional instruction using the same weekly problem sets (n = 68). Students’ solutions were scored with a validated analytic rubric aligned with the four Pólya stages, and outcomes were analyzed using ANCOVA with pre-test adjustment and a multilevel sensitivity model for section-level clustering. Results showed a statistically significant adjusted between-group difference favoring the GenAI-supported group, F(1, 125) = 28.76, p < .001, partial eta squared = .187, with the largest stage-specific effects for carrying out the plan and understanding the problem. Student perceptions were highly positive, and cognitive engagement showed the strongest association with performance gains. The study contributes to educational psychology by specifying a testable instructional mechanism: structured GenAI-supported instruction may support mathematical problem solving when prompts elicit planning, monitoring, explanation, and reflection while discouraging direct solution-seeking.

documents.abstract: Introduction The widespread application of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in knowledge-intensive domains requires continuous adjustment of human cognitive patterns. In terminology work, aligning strict semantic standards against the non-deterministic output of large language models (LLMs) is closely intertwined with workers' subjective cognitive load. This study examines the structural associations among prompt strategy preference, AI interaction self-efficacy, and subjective cognitive load, while testing the potential moderating role of professional experience. Methods Based on cross-sectional survey data from 1,760 practitioners using LLMs for terminology tasks, structural equation modeling (SEM) and latent profile analysis (LPA) were employed. SEM evaluated the linear structural associations among prompt strategy preference, self-efficacy, and cognitive load, while LPA identified behavioral user profiles. Multi-group equivalence testing was further conducted across three career stages (novices, intermediates, and experts). Results Prompt strategy preference is significantly and negatively associated with subjective cognitive load, with AI interaction self-efficacy serving as a significant mediator in this structural relationship. LPA identified three distinct user profiles (low, medium, and high strategy use), with the high strategy group exhibiting the lowest cognitive load and highest self-efficacy. Multi-group equivalence tests indicated no statistically significant moderation across experience cohorts, demonstrating structural invariance of the core model across career stages. Discussion From the perspective of cognitive ergonomics, upfront prompt structuring is structurally linked to downstream cognitive offloading and psychological buffering. These findings provide empirical evidence for individual cognitive resilience during human-AI collaboration in the generative AI era.

Purpose: This study develops a governance architecture for board-governed strategic decisions in which artificial intelligence (AI) provides common advice while legal and organizational decision ownership remains human. It examines two linked risks: erosion of independent human information and distortion of delegation through outcome-dependent credit and blame. Methodology/Approach: A theoretical decision-economic model is used to formalize firm-optimal and executive-optimal delegation, an endogenous attribution wedge, common-AI-induced error covariance, and boundary conditions for pre-AI information recording. The analysis treats governance controls as ex-ante commitments rather than ex-post corrections. Findings: Common exposure to an imperfect AI signal can increase correlation among revised human judgments and reduce the effective number of independent checks. Separately, private attribution incentives can move delegation away from the firm-optimal benchmark. The proposed Information Lock records designated human assessments before common AI exposure, while the Accountability Lock fixes effective decision rights and attribution rules before outcomes are known. The model also identifies limits: perfectly reconstructible post-AI judgments reduce the Information Lock mainly to an auditability device, while residual career downside can shift distortion from over-delegation toward rejection or delay of positive-value decisions. Conclusion: The contribution is a unified, selective governance architecture linking information independence and outcome-invariant accountability. It provides boards and senior executives with an implementable framework for preserving informational diversity, clarifying decision ownership, and distinguishing poor process from unfavorable stochastic outcomes in AI-assisted strategic decisions.
